claims.assertion: There is exactly one off-route segment in this trip: 09:04–09:07, where 1.97 km was driven against 0.21 km of optimal route, adding 1.76 km (max 957 m off the optimal route); total actual distance was 11.7 km vs 9.9 km optimal, so the entire claimed +1.8 km excess is attributable to that single three-minute segment.

That segment is exempt under RD-4(a): an LTA DataMall accident was reported at 08:44 on the Tampines Expressway towards Tampines Mall, 0 m from the optimal route, with lanes blocked; the report precedes the 09:04 start of the off-route segment and lies inside the trip window, so there was reasonable cause for the diversion.

The traffic record independently corroborates the blockage: Tampines Expressway was recorded at speed band 1 (0–9 km/h, severe congestion) during 08:46–09:04, i.e. covering exactly the stretch of the optimal route immediately before the diversion, which is the road the driver avoided.

The rider never asked for a stop or a change of destination in the chat (the only messages are the rider's 08:52 pickup note and the driver's arrival reply), so no part of the diversion is being excused as a rider-requested route change; the driver's case rests solely on the documented traffic obstruction in D2–D3.

The only distance-related amount in the bill that could be disputed is the excess-distance line of $2.55 (1.8 km × $1.41/km) inside the $27.27 metered total, and because the sole off-route segment is exempt under RD-4 no portion of that amount is refundable — the correct outcome is no_action rather than refund_partial.

No other charge in the metered fare is contestable: waiting was $0.00, the platform fee is a published $1.47 item, the base $3.90 and time $5.33 are metered units, and there was no surge (1.0×) and no manual post-trip add-on, so FARE-1 leaves nothing to refund.

The congestion was purely road-related, not weather-related: weather at the time was Fair with 0.0 mm rain, so the slowdown on the optimal route came from the reported accident and lane blockage, not adverse conditions the driver should have anticipated.

The driver's 90-day record shows 4 disputes but 0 route disputes upheld and 0 no-show disputes upheld, so RD-6's precondition (route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1) is not met and no flag_account may be attached to this case even if a route violation is recorded.

weaknesses: The GPS shows the segment physically left the optimal route by up to 957 m and added 1.76 km (F1, F3), so on the face of the data the driver breached the RD-1 duty to take the shortest and most direct route; the rider will lean on F1/F3 and argue the diversion was unnecessary.

The diversion ran 09:04–09:07 while the accident was reported at 08:44 (F13) and the band-1 congestion window on Tampines Expressway ended at 09:04 (F10) — the rider can argue the driver started the detour exactly as congestion was clearing, i.e. after the cause had ended, and that no traffic fact specifically covers the 09:04–09:07 detour window itself.

Under RD-4(b) a speed band alone (F10) cannot independently exempt a segment, so if the judge reads F13 as not matching the diverted stretch of the optimal route within the matching radius, the segment falls to RD-2 and the excess-distance line of $2.55 (F4) becomes refundable to the rider.

The driver's explanation is only a statement (F9) with no in-app notification to the rider, and the chat (F7, F8) shows no route discussion before leaving the optimal route, so RD-5 consent is unavailable and the whole defence depends on the traffic facts (F13, F10).

If the judge instead finds a route violation, the driver's 4 disputes in 90 days (F16) — albeit 0 route disputes upheld — could still invite scrutiny of his account, although RD-6's flag_account threshold is not met.

claims.assertion: The driver deviated from the optimal route: an off-route segment 09:04–09:07 covered 1.97 km where the optimal route covers 0.21 km, adding 1.76 km and straying up to 957 m from the route, which is the unexempted detour the rider complains about.

The detour is not excused by the driver's claim of an accident, because the accident record sits on the optimal route at 0 m from it and was reported 08:44, before the 09:04 detour began — the driver's own written statement (F9) is contradicted by the timing of the road block, and the speed band 1 record for Tampines Expressway ends at 09:04, exactly when he left the route.

The rider never agreed to a route change: the chat contains only pickup-location messages at 08:52 (F7, F8) and no message from the driver proposing an alternative route before 09:04, so there is no passenger consent pre-dating the off-route segment.

The congestion records on the alternative roads (Punggol Road and Tampines Avenue 12, both band 4, 30–39 km/h) are not on the replaced portion of the optimal route and are therefore not valid justification for the detour.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip, so the extra kilometres directly entered the fare: billed distance was 11.8 km and the excess 1.8 km was billed at $2.55 (1.8 km × $1.41/km), which is the recoverable amount for the 1.76 km unexempted detour.

The driver's 90-day history shows 4 disputes with 2 upheld, so if his account history includes a prior upheld route dispute a flag_account review is warranted alongside the refund; this profile fact is offered only as an additional action, not as the finding itself.

weaknesses: The driver will rely on F13 and F10: an accident on Tampines Expressway with lanes blocked, 0 m from the optimal route, reported 08:44, and speed band 1 (0–9 km/h) on that expressway — this is exactly the RD-4(a) type of evidence, and he will argue the block was still in force at 09:04 when he rerouted.

The excess billed per the fare record is 1.8 km (F4) while the single detected off-route segment adds 1.76 km (F3), so a small residual difference is not recoverable and the judge may round the refund down; the policy also only refunds the distance units, not the time component ($5.33 for 20.5 min) or the base/platform fees.

The rider's own evidence is limited to the absence of a chat agreement (F7, F8): there is no message from the rider objecting during the trip, so the driver may argue the rider silently acquiesced by not protesting.
Driver profile (F16) records 0 route disputes upheld in 90 days, so the RD-6 flag_account attachment is not clearly triggered on this record.

claims.assertion: There is exactly one off-route segment in this trip: 09:04–09:07, where 1.97 km was driven against 0.21 km of optimal route, adding 1.76 km (max 957 m off the optimal route); total actual distance was 11.7 km vs 9.9 km optimal, so the entire claimed +1.8 km excess is attributable to that single three-minute segment.

That segment is exempt under RD-4(a): an LTA DataMall accident was reported at 08:44 on the Tampines Expressway towards Tampines Mall, 0 m from the optimal route, with lanes blocked; the report precedes the 09:04 start of the off-route segment and lies inside the trip window, so there was reasonable cause for the diversion.

The traffic record independently corroborates the blockage: Tampines Expressway was recorded at speed band 1 (0–9 km/h, severe congestion) during 08:46–09:04, i.e. covering exactly the stretch of the optimal route immediately before the diversion, which is the road the driver avoided.

The rider never asked for a stop or a change of destination in the chat (the only messages are the rider's 08:52 pickup note and the driver's arrival reply), so no part of the diversion is being excused as a rider-requested route change; the driver's case rests solely on the documented traffic obstruction in D2–D3.

The only distance-related amount in the bill that could be disputed is the excess-distance line of $2.55 (1.8 km × $1.41/km) inside the $27.27 metered total, and because the sole off-route segment is exempt under RD-4 no portion of that amount is refundable — the correct outcome is no_action rather than refund_partial.

No other charge in the metered fare is contestable: waiting was $0.00, the platform fee is a published $1.47 item, the base $3.90 and time $5.33 are metered units, and there was no surge (1.0×) and no manual post-trip add-on, so FARE-1 leaves nothing to refund.

The congestion was purely road-related, not weather-related: weather at the time was Fair with 0.0 mm rain, so the slowdown on the optimal route came from the reported accident and lane blockage, not adverse conditions the driver should have anticipated.

The driver's 90-day record shows 4 disputes but 0 route disputes upheld and 0 no-show disputes upheld, so RD-6's precondition (route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1) is not met and no flag_account may be attached to this case even if a route violation is recorded.

weaknesses: The GPS shows the segment physically left the optimal route by up to 957 m and added 1.76 km (F1, F3), so on the face of the data the driver breached the RD-1 duty to take the shortest and most direct route; the rider will lean on F1/F3 and argue the diversion was unnecessary.

The diversion ran 09:04–09:07 while the accident was reported at 08:44 (F13) and the band-1 congestion window on Tampines Expressway ended at 09:04 (F10) — the rider can argue the driver started the detour exactly as congestion was clearing, i.e. after the cause had ended, and that no traffic fact specifically covers the 09:04–09:07 detour window itself.

Under RD-4(b) a speed band alone (F10) cannot independently exempt a segment, so if the judge reads F13 as not matching the diverted stretch of the optimal route within the matching radius, the segment falls to RD-2 and the excess-distance line of $2.55 (F4) becomes refundable to the rider.

The driver's explanation is only a statement (F9) with no in-app notification to the rider, and the chat (F7, F8) shows no route discussion before leaving the optimal route, so RD-5 consent is unavailable and the whole defence depends on the traffic facts (F13, F10).

If the judge instead finds a route violation, the driver's 4 disputes in 90 days (F16) — albeit 0 route disputes upheld — could still invite scrutiny of his account, although RD-6's flag_account threshold is not met.

RD-4(a) requires the traffic incident to cover the replaced portion of the optimal route and to still apply during the diversion: the accident was reported at 08:44 on Tampines Expressway (F13), but the off-route segment only runs 09:04–09:07 (F3), and no traffic fact places any obstruction on the optimal route during 09:04–09:07, so the exemption fails at the time it is needed.

The band-1 record on Tampines Expressway expires at 09:04 (F10) — the very minute the diversion began (F3) — and RD-4(b) says a speed band alone cannot exempt a segment even when it overlaps, so this evidence confirms congestion was ending, not that a detour was needed for 09:04–09:07.

We agree no rider-requested change exists (F7, F8), which removes the RD-3/RD-5 defence entirely and leaves the driver's justification resting on traffic facts that do not cover the 09:04–09:07 window (F3, F13); the rider's silence is not consent because the driver never proposed a route change before leaving the optimal route.

RD-2's non-exemption branch applies once RD-4 fails: on this RydeTAXI trip the extra kilometres enter the meter, and the recoverable amount is the unexempted segment's 1.76 km valued at the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (F4, F6), i.e. refund_partial of $2.55, with the residual ≤0.25 km map-matching difference left with the rider.

Conceded: the driver's record shows 0 route disputes upheld in 90 days (F16), so RD-6's flag_account precondition is not met and the rider does not press for a flag_account; the refund claim stands on RD-2 alone.
